slides.headline: Your pelvic floor: more than squeezing
slides.sub: What clinical Pilates teaches about lifting, letting go and breathing.

slides.title: What the pelvic floor does
slides.body: It's a group of muscles at the base of your pelvis. They support the bladder and bowel, help with continence, and work together with your breathing and deep trunk muscles.

slides.title: Letting go matters too
slides.body: Pelvic floor muscles need to lift and relax. Some people hold too much tension, which can cause its own problems. Clinical Pilates teaches both the gentle lift and the release.

slides.title: Breathe with it
slides.body: As you breathe in, the pelvic floor gently lowers. As you breathe out, it lifts a little. Pilates uses this rhythm to time the effort of an exercise with your out-breath.

slides.title: Build it into real movement
slides.body: Once you can find the muscles, the aim is using them in daily tasks like squatting, lifting and getting out of the car. Reformer work lets you progress this gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Leaking, a heavy or dragging feeling, pelvic pain, or pain during intercourse are worth discussing with your GP or a pelvic health physiotherapist before starting a program.

slides.headline: Start with a Pilates assessment
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team checks how you move and breathe, then builds a program around you. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Pelvic floor training isn't just about squeezing as hard as you can.

These muscles support your bladder and bowel and work alongside your breath and deep trunk muscles. They need to lift, but they also need to let go, and some people hold far too much tension.

Clinical Pilates can help you coordinate the two: a gentle lift on the out-breath, a full release on the in-breath, then building that into squats, lifting and everyday movement. Leaking, heaviness or pelvic pain are worth discussing with your GP or a pelvic health physiotherapist first.
